title: European Conflict & Security Intelligence
tagline: Conflict events and defence budgets in Europe, side by side — then a pre-specified event study of whether proximity to Russia predicts the rise in military burden.
role: Solo — data pipeline, geospatial and econometric analysis, dashboard

hero.alt: Dashboard page showing recorded conflict events in Europe per month from 2014 to 2025, with headline figures for events, countries, estimated fatalities and the share of precisely located events
hero.caption: Conflict patterns from UCDP GED. Every headline figure states its denominator, and counts are labelled as recorded events, not a census of what happened.

problem: Conflict and defence data are easy to chart and easy to misread. Event counts move when reporting changes, fatality figures are wide estimates, and spending series mix price bases. Put conflict and spending on one chart and it invites a causal story the data cannot support.
data: The **UCDP Georeferenced Event Dataset** (58,016 European events, 1989–2025) and the **SIPRI Military Expenditure Database**, each file recorded with URL, retrieval time and SHA-256. ACLED is supported but never redistributed, as its licence requires.
built: A validated DuckDB pipeline with machine-readable quality reports and a GeoPandas point-in-country check; the code refuses invalid operations such as growth on current prices.

On top, an event study written down before any estimate: military burden in 37 countries, 2005–2025, against each capital's distance to Russia, with two-way fixed effects and a wild cluster bootstrap.

images.alt: Line chart of estimated fatalities per year in Europe from 1989 to 2025, with a shaded band between UCDP's low and high estimates that widens sharply after 2022
images.caption: UCDP's best estimate with its low–high range. For 2022 the high estimate is 2.4 times the low, so point figures for an active war are not quoted without the band.

images.alt: Map of Getis-Ord Gi* hot spots of recorded conflict events in 2022 to 2025 on a 25 km equal-area grid, showing a narrow band of significant cells along eastern Ukraine and a smaller cluster near Kherson, with grey cells for non-significant locations with events
images.caption: Gi* hot spots, 2022–2025, on 25 km equal-area cells with false-discovery-rate correction: 82% of precisely located events fall in cells covering under 3% of the study area.

images.alt: Event-study chart of the yearly gradient of military expenditure in percent of GDP per 1,000 km from Russia, near zero before 2014, drifting down after 2014 and falling sharply after 2022, with 95 percent confidence intervals
images.caption: Year-by-year gradient relative to 2013. Near zero before 2014, drifting down after the annexation of Crimea, and breaking sharply after the full-scale invasion.

images.alt: Dashboard page showing military expenditure in constant 2024 US dollars for six European countries from 2000 to 2025, with the unit and price basis stated above the chart
images.caption: Defence trends from SIPRI. The unit and price basis are always displayed, and SIPRI estimates are marked rather than blended in.

images.alt: Bar chart of the number of European countries with military expenditure at or above 2 percent of GDP each year, shown against the number of countries with data
images.caption: European countries at or above 2% of GDP, against the number with data each year. SIPRI's definition differs from NATO's, so this is not a compliance measure.

result: After 2022, burden rose **0.44 pp of GDP more per 1,000 km closer to Russia** (bootstrap p < 0.001), robust to every pre-specified check. The post-2014 gradient is weaker and fails its pre-trend test, and the write-up says so. Separately, the 2025 drop in recorded events turned out to be a coding change, not de-escalation.
technical: The point-in-country test flagged 1,177 events outside their stated country's present-day border. Almost all turned out to be UCDP's historical state coding — 1990s events in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo recorded under "Serbia (Yugoslavia)". That is a property of the source, not an error, but it changes what a country filter means.

The hot-spot layer runs Getis-Ord Gi* on an equal-area grid that keeps every zero-event cell inside the study area — dropping them is the classic error that makes every busy cell look ordinary — and corrects thousands of simultaneous tests with a false discovery rate. It matches PySAL to ten decimal places, and the cell-size dependence is reported at 10, 25 and 50 km rather than hidden.

Totals across countries use a balanced panel, so a country's series starting part-way through cannot inflate growth. The research brief is generated from the database and pinned to the input file hashes; it warns when the data have changed since the commentary was written. 53 tests run in CI, including a headless render of every dashboard page.

The estimator is plain numpy OLS so that 9,999 bootstrap draws reuse one design matrix (about 0.1 s); it is tested against statsmodels to machine precision, checked for correct size under a simulated null, and shown to recover a planted effect. Robustness covers levels instead of shares, war-event distance, a NATO control, dropping the Baltic states, leave-one-out and a placebo year. A randomization test that permutes distances across countries (p < 0.001) and a synthetic control for the Baltic states — 1.5 pp of GDP above a distant-country comparison after 2022, first among 21 placebos — confirm the gradient, while Estonia, Latvia and Poland individually cannot be separated from placebo noise, and the write-up says so.
